sentences.text: Adult Simosuchus measured approximately 0.75 meters in length, though some sources estimate the size at roughly 1 meter based on mature skeletons.
The animal is nicknamed the "pug-nosed crocodile" because its snout resembles that of a pug, a feature reflected in the genus name Simosuchus.
The skull of Simosuchus contains 45 autapomorphies, or unique features not found in other species.
Researchers initially suggested Simosuchus was a burrowing animal based on its robust limbs and short, shovel-like snout.
The type species Simosuchus clarki was discovered in the Maevarano Formation within Mahajanga Province, and the first known specimen served for its initial description in 2000.
The genus Simosuchus was described by Buckley et al. in 2000, and it was initially classified in the family Notosuchidae when described by them.
An isolated tooth of Simosuchus was found in the Kallamedu Formation in India.
There are 21 recorded fossil occurrences of Simosuchus.
Simosuchus was fully terrestrial, and its short tail suggests it was not adapted for swimming.
The inflexible osteoderm shield of Simosuchus likely restricted lateral movement as an adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle.
Unlike most other notosuchians, Simosuchus had semierect hindlimbs rather than a fully erect posture.
Due to its semi-erect posture, Simosuchus probably could not run.
Many paleontologists classify Simosuchus as a herbivore based on its dental and cranial morphology, while others believe it was a terrestrial omnivore based on its nail-shaped teeth and short snout.
Adult Simosuchus clarki may have been prey for adult Madtsoia madagascariensis snakes, though such large prey would likely have injured the snakes.
Simosuchus was initially classified as a basal member of the clade Notosuchia, and it belongs to the parent group Eunotosuchia.
Many Simosuchus remains were found as part of the Mahajanga Basin Project, directed by the University of Antananarivo and Stony Brook University.
It is unknown how Simosuchus arrived in Madagascar.

It is debated whether Simosuchus belongs within Notosuchia or is the sister taxon of the Chinese genus Chimaerasuchus in the family Chimaerasuchidae. It has been proposed that Simosuchus may have had a fossorial or digging lifestyle, but this is not widely accepted, even though evidence for a possible digging lifestyle includes Simosuchus's robust limbs and short, shovel-shaped snout. In 2010, Kley and colleagues argued against the burrowing hypothesis, stating the animal's morphology did not show adaptations for head-first burrowing.
